lead.title: Sixty-two per cent of family offices give household staff no security training, and only 4 per cent call what they offer sufficient
lead.standfirst: A new survey of family office security finds that the people closest to a principal are the least prepared, even as targeting of wealthy families rises.
lead.body:
The State of Family Office Security 2026, a 103-page study by Presage Global and Nines, reports that 62 per cent of family offices provide no formal security training to household staff. Only 4 per cent say the training they do provide is sufficient. The findings were reported by Family Wealth Report on 24 June 2026.

The gap matters because of how threats now arrive. AI-powered attacks are the top emerging concern for 65 per cent of respondents, and a convincing voice, email or message aimed at a driver, a housekeeper or an assistant is often cheaper to attempt than a breach of the principal's own systems. Yet only 7 per cent of respondents provide formal cybersecurity training to family members, so the weakness is not confined to the staff room.

The survey also shows how reactive most households remain. Some 47 per cent of family offices have never conducted a risk assessment, or conduct one only after an incident. Sixty per cent of security improvements follow an incident, against 19 per cent triggered by regular assessments, and the group that acts only reactively reported the highest incident rate, at 45 per cent.

The commercial signs point the same way. Dale Buckner, chief executive of Global Guardian, told Family Wealth Report that the firm's revenues rose 47 per cent year on year in 2025 and its executive protection work grew 71 per cent. He said targeting of high-net-worth individuals has increased even as overall crime in the United States has fallen, with organised groups using sophisticated methods.
lead.why: For an estate manager, security awareness is becoming part of the job description: someone who can brief a household on verification calls, visitor protocols and device hygiene is more valuable than the survey suggests most families have.

articles.title: Henley drops its millionaire headcount and ranks countries on how well they compete for mobile wealth
articles.body:
Henley & Partners published its Private Wealth Migration Report 2026 in June with a changed method. According to analysis from The Family Office Almanac, it no longer gives a precise count of millionaires moving between countries, saying the data does not yet support one, and its single named author has been removed. The headline is now a Wealth Mobility Competitiveness Score out of 100.

The change follows years of criticism. Dan Neidle of Tax Policy Associates and the Tax Justice Network had questioned the reliability of the earlier headcounts, particularly the figures on the United Kingdom. The new report instead says applications to Henley's own migration services from people with a UK address rose about 15 per cent over 2024 and 2025, a different measure from the earlier outflow claims.

On the scores, as reported by Wealth Professional, the United Arab Emirates leads at 85.3 and has been the top destination for relocating millionaires for two years. Singapore scores 79.5, New Zealand 75.8, the Cayman Islands 74.3 and Cyprus 73.5. The United Kingdom scores 68.3 and France 65.7, while the United States scores 62.3. The report describes a paradox in which the United States is both the largest private wealth market and the largest source of applications for residence or citizenship elsewhere.

Henley's central message is multijurisdictional living: wealthy families spreading residence, citizenship and business interests across several countries rather than anchoring to one. Enquiries from UAE-based individuals rose 41 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, as residents prepared contingency options amid regional conflict.
articles.why: A family holding several residences and passports needs a household that can open, close and move between them; understanding why principals diversify helps whoever runs the logistics.
articles.src: The Family Office Almanac / Wealth Professional

articles.title: Hong Kong's autumn auctions pass HK$2 billion as younger buyers arrive
articles.body:
Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips held their autumn marquee sales in Hong Kong from 28 to 30 September, and the South China Morning Post reported on 1 October that they together topped HK$2 billion, about USD 255.8 million. The spring series had totalled HK$1.3 billion.

Christie's took HK$956.5 million, up 17 per cent on the year. Sotheby's took HK$956 million, up 35 per cent on its March series, with a 91 per cent sell-through rate and five artist records. Christie's also reported a 30 per cent rise in new young buyers and broad international participation.

The newspaper linked the results to steady demand for leading Western and Asian art and to competitive bidding for works fresh to the market with strong provenance. Works by Yayoi Kusama, however, received what the headline called a cool reception, a reminder that even a rising market is selective.

The lead image of the report was Leonard Tsuguharu Foujita's Chatte et chaton of 1932, sold at Sotheby's on 28 September.
articles.why: Collections are managed as living assets, and a manager who knows which markets are firming and which names are cooling can speak credibly to advisers, registrars and the family.

articles.title: Lürssen delivered six yachts totalling 655 metres in 105 days this spring
articles.body:
Superyachts.com reported on 29 July that the German builder Lürssen delivered six yachts between March and June 2026, in 105 days, with a combined length of 655 metres. Five of the six exceed 100 metres, and the yard says it has built more than 30 yachts above that length.

The largest was Deep Blue at 134.2 metres, about which few official details have been released. Boardwalk measures 117 metres and Nausicaä 114.2 metres, the latter with exterior design by Marc Newson. O3, at 109 metres, was built for long-range exploration including Greenland and Antarctica. Nixie, at 102.4 metres, made her public debut at the Monaco Yacht Show and carries a six-metre glass pool, while Odisea, at 78.2 metres, favours a beach club over a traditional saloon.

The article names no owners and gives no crew numbers. Peter Lürssen called delivering six yachts in one year a remarkable achievement.
articles.why: Every delivery of this size brings a new crew, a new household afloat and new demands on shore teams, from provisioning to port agents and guest transfers.

briefs.t: Italy's flat tax stays in view as the UAE wobbles
briefs.b: Henley data cited by EnterpriseAM showed enquiries for Italy's residence programme up 5 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first of 2026. The regime lets foreign residents pay a flat EUR 300,000 a year on overseas income.

briefs.t: Gulf residents build a second option
briefs.b: Henley says applications for alternative residence or citizenship from UAE-based individuals rose 29 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first of 2026. It describes the shift as optionality rather than departure.

briefs.t: Executive protection is the fastest growing line
briefs.b: Global Guardian reports its executive protection work grew 71 per cent in 2025, ahead of 47 per cent growth in total revenues. Its chief executive attributes the rise to organised groups targeting wealthy individuals.
